title: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) for severe depression
description: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is given under general anaesthesia, usually two or three times a week, and is used mainly for severe depression that has not improved with other treatments. Scans before and after a course of ECT show the hippocampus and amygdala growing slightly in volume. In this episode brightness stands for tissue volume, not activity. In the first part it shows how volume differed from people without depression before treatment; in "What changed" it shows the change since before treatment.
caveat: The volume increase comes from a combined analysis of 281 patients at 10 sites and from a study of 43 patients. The increase is small, a few percent, and grows with the number of sessions. The larger analysis found that a bigger increase did not go with a better outcome, so the growth does not explain why ECT works. Only the hippocampus and amygdala were measured in these studies. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: A larger increase in the hippocampus did not go with a better outcome in the largest analysis, so the change in size does not explain the benefit. In people without depression scanned twice, the measurements stayed the same.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: Smaller than in people without depression before treatment, in one study. Larger after a course of ECT, in that study and in a combined analysis of 281 patients, by about 0.28% per session. The larger increase did not go with a better outcome. Brightness stands for volume, not activity.
